Arians later appealed to Wisdom’s speech as evidence that Christ was created. The orthodox response required interpreting the personification of Wisdom in light of the New Testament’s teaching about the eternal Son; the word *archē* alone cannot settle that Christological question. The relationship to Colossians 1:15 and Revelation 3:14 will become clear below.

contains: The NET renders Wisdom’s words
replacement: *The Proverbs 8:22 Arian appeal.* The BSB renders Wisdom’s words, “The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old.” The Septuagint uses *ektisen* and *archēn*. Arius and his followers identified Wisdom directly with Christ and used the verse to argue that the Son was created. The orthodox response reads this poetic personification alongside the clearer teaching of John 1:1, Colossians 1:15–18, and Hebrews 1. A figurative speech by Wisdom cannot overturn those passages’ teaching about the Son. The dispute concerns the interpretation and Christological application of the passage, not merely which English word is chosen for *archē*.

contains: The NET's phrase *careful regard*

contains: The NET reads, “Every scripture is inspired by God

contains: The NET renders the opening of the verse:

Those terms direct attention to related questions: how sin is dealt with, how divine judgment is answered, and where God meets sinners in mercy. This study argues that the word’s sacrificial background belongs with the Lutheran confession that Christ bore our sin and God’s judgment against it. That argument must be made from the passage and its biblical context; it should not be made to depend on one English rendering.

contains: The NET uses “acknowledges” here

The faith that confesses Christ before men finds Christ confessing it before God; the faith that denies Christ before men finds itself denied. The Christian’s public speech is not optional; the New Testament treats it as integral to discipleship.

contains: which the NET renders “born from above,”
replacement: *Paliggenesia* is not the only New Testament term for regeneration. Jesus uses *gennēthē anōthen* in John 3:3 and 3:7, which the BSB renders “born again,” and speaks of being “born of water and the Spirit” in John 3:5. Peter uses *anagennaō*: God “has given us new birth” (1 Peter 1:3, BSB), and “you have been born again” (1 Peter 1:23, BSB). These expressions concern the new life God gives, with different emphases in their respective contexts.

contains: The NET’s “the age when all things are renewed”
replacement: The cosmic *paliggenesia*. The BSB's “the renewal of all things” renders *en tē paliggenesia*—“in the regeneration.” Jesus is speaking of the consummation, when He will sit on His throne of glory and all things will be made new. The twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones; the eschatological renewal will be the setting; the *paliggenesia* names the whole. This use connects to the broader New Testament hope for the renewal of all things (Acts 3:21, Romans 8:18–25, Revelation 21:1–5). The cosmos itself is on the way to *paliggenesia*; what God does in the individual believer now is the foretaste and pledge of what He will do for the whole creation then.

contains: the NET renders the phrase as Israel's *restoration*

contains: Compare the NET’s “what has been entrusted to me”

Paul writes that he is convinced God is able to guard *tēn parathēkēn mou*—“my deposit”—until that day. A possessive genitive can point either direction. It may mean *the deposit I have made with Him*: Paul has handed his life, work, and death over to God for safekeeping. It may mean *the deposit He has made with me*: the gospel Paul was given, which God Himself will preserve. The BSB chooses the first: “what I have entrusted to Him.” The direction of the entrusting is an interpretive decision. Both readings are grammatically available and theologically coherent; the verse is one of the places where a translator has to choose and the reader deserves to be told that a choice was made. The immediate context, where verse 14 clearly means the gospel entrusted to Timothy, gives a mild edge to the second reading. It is an edge, not a proof.

replacement: The BSB reflects this difficulty: Galatians 4 uses *basic principles*, while Colossians 2 uses *spiritual forces*. A careful entry should acknowledge the alternatives rather than declare one English gloss sufficient for every passage.

The BSB presents Hosea's words as a declaration of ransom and redemption followed by “Compassion is hidden from My eyes”; the verse's punctuation and force have been understood differently. Paul's resurrection argument gives the taunt against death its triumphant setting: the victory is grounded in what God has done through our Lord Jesus Christ.

replacement: The dispute concerns the last clause, *theos ēn ho logos*. The Jehovah’s Witness interpretation treats the Word as a lesser divine being. contains: The NET calls them wounds.
replacement: John 20:25 uses the noun for the nail marks in Jesus' hands, and the BSB retains *marks*. That concrete use helps us hear the word before it becomes a term in a Bible-study method. A *typos* can be something recognizable and definite, not merely a resemblance someone has imagined.

contains: The NET reads: “Now faith is being sure
replacement: English Bibles render Hebrews 11:1 in different ways. The BSB reads: “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” Other renderings use words such as *substance* and *confidence*. These choices reflect the breadth of *hypostasis* and the question of how it describes faith’s relation to what God has promised. The rest of this study examines that range of meaning and the word’s later use in the church’s confession of Christ and the Trinity.

contains: The NET’s “his essence” translates
replacement: The substantive use. The BSB's “His nature” translates *tēs hypostaseōs autou*—“His *hypostasis*.” Christ is the *charaktēr*—the exact stamp or imprint, like the impression a seal makes on wax—of God’s *hypostasis*. The image is concrete: Christ bears the imprint of God’s own being in such a way that to see Christ is to see God. Hebrews 1:3 is one of the foundational New Testament texts for the deity of Christ, sitting alongside John 1:1, Philippians 2:6, and Colossians 1:15–20. Christ is not merely a creature who reflects God’s character at a distance; Christ bears the very imprint of the divine being itself. The Greek word *charaktēr* (from which the English “character” descends) was used for the imprint a die makes on a coin—exact, precise, of the same substance as what stamped it. Christ is to God the Father what the imprint on a coin is to the die that stamped it: not a different reality but a precise impression of the same.

contains: The NET’s “our initial confidence”
replacement: The subjective use. The BSB's “our original conviction” translates *tēn archēn tēs hypostaseōs*—“the beginning of our *hypostasis*.” The believer’s *hypostasis* is the firm standing he has in Christ from the time of his initial faith. The exhortation is to hold this *hypostasis* firm to the end—to maintain the original confidence that the gospel produced when faith first took hold. The author of Hebrews uses *hypostasis* here in the psychological-confidence sense: the believer’s settled assurance, his firm standing in Christ, his unwavering commitment that must be maintained through the trials of Christian life.

contains: the NET’s “being sure of what we hope for.”
replacement: The subjective reading (favored by most modern translations and by much modern scholarship) takes *hypostasis* in the confidence sense: faith is the believer’s settled conviction about realities he cannot yet see—the BSB's “assurance of what we hope for.” On this reading, *hypostasis* names the believer’s confident stance, paralleling the *elenchos* (“conviction”) in the second half of the verse.

contains: The NET’s “confidence” renders *tē hypostasei tautē*
replacement: Paul on the collection for Jerusalem. The BSB's “confidence” renders *tē hypostasei tautē*—“in this *hypostasis*,” in this firm standing or confidence. Paul has been boasting to the Macedonians about the Corinthians’ readiness to give; if the Corinthians fail to come through, the *hypostasis* of Paul’s boasting will be exposed as empty. The use is clearly the subjective sense—confident standing, firm commitment, the basis on which one makes a claim.

contains: names the Son as “the representation of his essence” in the NET
replacement: First, the believer’s faith has a foundation that is not the believer’s own subjective state but the objective reality of Christ Himself. Hebrews 1:3 names the Son as “the exact representation of His nature” in the BSB; *hypostasis* here concerns God’s own being. The believer who has Christ has, in some real sense, access to the imprint of God’s own being. The *hypostasis* the believer rests on is not his own conviction; it is Christ Himself.

contains: The NET renders Hebrews 11:1
replacement: The BSB renders Hebrews 11:1 as “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” This foregrounds confident trust. The lexical discussion of *hypostasis* also raises the question of the reality on which that confidence rests. The theological point is not that one English word proves both readings, but that Christian faith trusts what God has promised and accomplished in Christ. Its confidence has an object beyond the believer’s changing feelings.

contains: *Proverbs 1:8, 4:1* —
replacement: *Proverbs 1:8; 4:1* — “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.” / “Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding.” The wisdom tradition's foundational pattern: the older teaching the younger.

contains: Jeremiah 3:4 —

Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.” The verb is present tense. The believer already has the life. The resurrection of the body will reveal what is now hidden. First John 5:13 — “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.” Present possession, future consummation. Both are real.

contains: Second, the dwelling of God with His people.
replacement: Second, the dwelling of God with His people. *Idou hē skēnē tou theou meta tōn anthrōpōn* — “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3, BSB). The new creation is fundamentally about God dwelling with His people. The covenant formula ([Laos](/greek/laos/)) reaches its consummation: “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.” The new creation is the place of unmediated communion between God and His people.

contains: The last verse of Acts. *Meta pasēs parrhēsias akōlytōs*

Luke ends his narrative not with martyrdom or triumph but with Paul preaching openly to anyone who will come, in the capital of the empire, under house arrest. The *parrhēsia* persists even in chains. This is one of the strongest endings in all of literature, and the word *parrhēsia* carries much of its weight.

contains: The verse also names what Scripture is *not*:
replacement: The verse also names what Scripture is *not*: no prophecy of Scripture “comes from one’s own interpretation” (2 Peter 1:20, BSB), and no prophecy “was ever brought forth by the will of man” (2 Peter 1:21, BSB). The Spirit's work in the human authors means that Scripture is not reducible to the human authors' opinions. The result is more than the sum of the human contributors.

*Luke 24:25–27, 44–49.* The Emmaus road narrative (already quoted in the entry's hook), continued at the upper room appearance: “Then Jesus said to them, ‘O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?’ And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. … Jesus said to them, ‘These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.’ Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. And He told them, ‘This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.’”

contains: The closing application is direct:
replacement: The closing application is direct: “Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.” The Christ-pattern is the believer's pattern. The contemplation of Christ's endurance is what sustains the believer's endurance. The believer who is in danger of growing weary needs to look at Christ — at His cross-endurance, at His vindication, at His present session at the Father's right hand. The looking produces the strength to continue.

contains: *All believers in Christ (the broad use in Acts).*
replacement: *All believers in Christ (the broad use in Acts).* The most theologically substantive use for our purposes. Acts uses *mathētēs* over thirty times for ordinary believers, not just the Twelve. Acts 6:1 — “In those days when the disciples were increasing in number, the Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.” Acts 6:7 — “So the word of God continued to spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem grew rapidly, and a great number of priests became obedient to the faith.” Acts 9:1, 19, 26 — Saul's encounters with "the disciples" in Damascus and Jerusalem. Acts 11:26 — “The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.” This broader use establishes the entire church as a community of *mathētai*.

contains: The third is the “love wins” reduction — love as universal acceptance
replacement: The third is the “love wins” reduction — love as universal acceptance with no moral content. This is the love that refuses to judge anything, accommodates every desire, blesses every choice. This is not what the New Testament means by love. The Christ who said “love your enemy” (Matthew 5:44, BSB) also said “Now go and sin no more” (John 8:11, BSB). Christian love calls people to repentance, holds boundaries, refuses to bless what God has not blessed. Love that does not speak truth is not the *agapē* of the New Testament. Paul names the standard explicitly: “the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15, BSB) — the two together, never separated.

contains: *Numbers 6:24-26* — The Aaronic blessing.
replacement: *Numbers 6:24–26* — The Aaronic blessing. “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.” The standard priestly blessing of Israel, still in use in confessional Lutheran worship as the closing benediction of the Divine Service. Three uses of *barak* (in the verb-forms) structure the threefold blessing.

contains: *Numbers 6:24-26 (and its New Testament continuation).*
replacement: *Numbers 6:24–26 (and its New Testament continuation).* “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.”

contains: The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the doctrine of inspiration.
replacement: The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the doctrine of inspiration. Most lay readers know the Bible is “the Word of God” but have not worked through what that means. Walk through two passages. 2 Timothy 3:16 — “All Scripture is God-breathed”; the Greek *theopneustos* names what Scripture *is*: produced by God’s own breath, not merely “deeply moving.” 2 Peter 1:21 — “no prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit”; the participle *pheromenoi* pictures the authors carried like a ship in the wind. Together they give the full doctrine: Scripture is fully human (real people wrote it, with their own vocabulary and personality) and fully divine (the Spirit carried them, so what they wrote is God’s breathed-out Word). This is what makes *sola Scriptura* coherent — Scripture alone as the norm, because Scripture alone is *theopneustos*.

contains: *Theopneustos* (θεόπνευστος) — God-breathed, inspired.
replacement: *Theopneustos* (θεόπνευστος) — God-breathed, inspired. The famous word from 2 Timothy 3:16 (“All Scripture is God-breathed”), built from *theos* + the *pneō* root (to breathe). A *hapax legomenon* (a word occurring only once) in the New Testament, but theologically foundational.

contains: *God's purpose is realized in Christ —
replacement: *God's purpose is realized in Christ — the Christological center of God's eternal plan grounds the believer's confidence.* Ephesians 1:9–11 (“which He purposed in Christ”), 3:11 (“the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord”), and 2 Timothy 1:9 (“by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began”). The eternal purpose is not an abstract decree about individuals apart from Christ; the eternal purpose is God's plan to unite all things in Christ.

contains: *Athanasia* (ἀθανασία) — immortality
replacement: *Athanasia* (ἀθανασία) — immortality (literally "without death," the *a-* privative prefix negating *thanatos*). Used at 1 Corinthians 15:53–54 (the resurrection body must "put on immortality") and at 1 Timothy 6:16 (“He alone is immortal”).

contains: The antinomian error treats the transfer as removing all obligation to the law
replacement: This emphasis distinguishes confessional Lutheran teaching from two opposite errors. The antinomian error treats the transfer as removing all obligation to the law — the believer is “like one without the law” in a way that exempts him from obedience, while Paul explicitly says he is “not outside the law of God but under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21, BSB). The legalistic error treats the transfer as conditional on the believer's continuing performance — the believer's status depends on his ongoing works. Lutheran teaching holds both: the transfer is by grace through faith (against legalism), and the transfer obligates the believer to active obedience (against antinomianism). The Formula of Concord Article VI (on the third use of the law) is the foundational confessional Lutheran treatment of this tension.

contains: First, the structural language. *Labein ex ethnōn laon*
replacement: First, the structural language. *Labein ex ethnōn laon* — “God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people to be His own.” The Greek is striking: God is *taking from the Gentiles* a *people*. The Gentiles (*ethnē* — nations, treated in [Ethnos](/greek/ethnos/)) are the broader category from which God is forming His people (*laos*). The two categories are distinct: not every Gentile becomes part of the *laos*; some are taken from among them to constitute God's people.

contains: *2 Timothy 1:10.*
replacement: *2 Timothy 1:10.* “And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel.” The backward-facing use. Note the two verbs of visibility stacked — *revealed*, *illuminated* — and note what is said to have been done to death: *katargēsantos*, rendered inoperative, put out of commission. The first appearing did not postpone death. It decommissioned it.

contains: *Genesis 14:18-20* — the appearance of Melchizedek
replacement: *Genesis 14:18–20* — the appearance of Melchizedek, who blesses Abraham: “Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High—and he blessed Abram and said: ‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.’ Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything.” This mysterious figure becomes important for Hebrews's development of Christ's priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.

contains: What is distinctive in Titus is the closing emphasis:
replacement: What is distinctive in Titus is the closing emphasis: the *episkopos* “must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” Oversight includes the doctrinal dimension explicitly — instruction in sound doctrine, refutation of error. The *episkopos* is not merely an administrator; he is a guardian of the gospel deposit, charged with teaching the truth and answering those who contradict it.

contains: The location of the anchor is theologically loaded.
replacement: The location of the anchor is theologically loaded. The anchor “enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain” — that is, into the Holy of Holies, the innermost chamber of the temple, where God's presence dwells. The image is striking: the believer's anchor extends past the visible world into God's own presence, where it is fastened to something the believer cannot see but that holds the believer steady against every storm. Christ Himself has gone into this inner place (Hebrews 6:20), and the believer's hope is anchored where Christ is.

contains: *The cosmic deceiver.*
replacement: *The cosmic deceiver.* The eschatological dimension. Satan as *ho planōn* (the one who deceives) the whole world. Revelation 12:9 names him “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.”

contains: *2 Timothy 1:10.*
replacement: *2 Timothy 1:10.* “And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel.” *Sōtēr* is attached to the first appearing and to the decommissioning of death.

contains: *Isaiah 49:6* —
replacement: *Isaiah 49:6* — “He says: ‘It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel. I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.’” The Servant's mission is not just to Israel but to the nations.

contains: The connections to the means of grace are direct.
replacement: The connections to the means of grace are direct. Baptism ([Baptizō](/greek/baptizo/)) is the entry into *zōē* — Romans 6:4 names the believer as walking “in newness of life” after baptismal union with Christ. The Lord’s Supper (see [Anamnesis](/greek/anamnesis/), [Soma](/greek/soma/), [Haima](/greek/haima/), [Artos](/greek/artos/), and [Koinonia](/greek/koinonia/)) sustains *zōē* — John 6:54 names the participant as having “eternal life” through feeding on Christ’s flesh and blood. The Spirit ([Pneuma](/greek/pneuma/)) is the giver of life — 2 Corinthians 3:6 says “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” and Romans 8:11 promises that the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to the believer’s mortal body. The Word ([Logos](/greek/logos/)) is the source of life — John 1:4, “in Him was life, and that life was the light of men.” The whole structure of Christian existence is grounded in the *zōē* of Christ given through the means Christ has appointed.

contains: *The apostolic deposit is to be guarded, preserved, and transmitted faithfully
replacement: *The apostolic deposit is to be guarded, preserved, and transmitted faithfully across generations.* Second Timothy 1:13–14 directs Timothy: “Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.” The pattern Paul gave to Timothy is the same pattern Timothy is to deliver to “faithful men who will be qualified to teach others” (2 Timothy 2:2, BSB). The transmission across generations is the church's task. Each generation receives what the previous generation has preserved, holds it faithfully, and delivers it to the next.

contains: *Ornament or adornment.*
replacement: *Ornament or adornment.* First Peter 3:3 says, “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes.” This is a specific but important sense, in which *kosmos* names the arrangement of jewelry or clothing for personal display. The verse exhorts Christian women to a different kind of *kosmos* — the inner adornment of a gentle spirit. The word is being used in two senses in the same passage: the external *kosmos* of jewelry, and the metaphorical *kosmos* of character.

contains: *The act of human judging.*
replacement: *The act of human judging.* John 7:24 (“Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly”), John 8:16 (“My judgment is true”).

contains: *Christ as the human being.*
replacement: *Christ as the human being.* The Christological usage. First Timothy 2:5 names “the man Christ Jesus” as the “one mediator between God and men.” Romans 5:15 says, “But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many!” Christ in His incarnate humanity is named with the same word that names every other human.

contains: The aorist participle *agorasanta*
replacement: The aorist participle *agorasanta* — “the Master who bought them” — applies to false teachers who are described as having been bought yet denying their Purchaser.

contains: *Blessing of those who curse or persecute.*
replacement: *Blessing of those who curse or persecute.* The believer's ethical practice. Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:28 — "bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you." Romans 12:14 — “Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse.” First Peter 3:9 — “Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.” The Christian ethic of blessing as the response to evil is one of the most striking New Testament reversals of natural human response.

contains: *The Abrahamic promise — that all the families of the earth
replacement: *The Abrahamic promise — that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham — is the foundational missional framework for biblical theology, and its fulfillment in Christ's mission to the nations is the basis for the church's continuing missional task.* Genesis 12:1–3, Matthew 28:18–20, and Galatians 3:8–9 (“The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you.’ So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith”). The mission to the nations is not a strategic decision the church made at some point; the mission is the realization of God's promise that runs from Genesis to Revelation.

contains: *Ezekiel 14:13* —
replacement: *Ezekiel 14:13* — “Son of man, if a land sins against Me by acting unfaithfully, and I stretch out My hand against it to cut off its supply of food, to send famine upon it, and to cut off from it both man and beast.” The covenant unfaithfulness of a nation is named *paraptōma* in the LXX.

contains: The crucial detail for understanding *kenoō* is the grammar of verse 7.
replacement: The crucial detail for understanding *kenoō* is the grammar of verse 7. Paul says Christ “emptied Himself” — *heauton ekenōsen* — and then attaches a participle that explains *how*: “taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness.” The participle tells us the manner of the emptying. Christ emptied Himself *by taking on* the form of a servant. The emptying is not a subtraction from His divinity. It is an addition of humanity. He did not become less God. He became also a servant. The kenosis *is* the incarnation.

contains: First, the emptying is the incarnation, not a subtraction of divinity.
replacement: First, the emptying is the incarnation, not a subtraction of divinity. Read Philippians 2:7 carefully. Paul does not say what Christ emptied Himself *of*. He says how Christ emptied Himself: “taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness.” The participle controls the verb. The emptying is the taking on. He did not become less God by adding humanity; He became God-and-servant, fully, both at once. The kenosis is incarnational addition, not divine subtraction.

contains: *Isaiah 61:1* —
replacement: *Isaiah 61:1* — “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners.” Christ identifies Himself with this prophecy at Luke 4:18–19, declaring the Jubilee fulfilled in His ministry.

contains: *Psalm 67:1* —
replacement: *Psalm 67:1* — “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm. A song. May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us, Selah.” A psalmic echo of the Aaronic blessing applied to the whole congregation.

contains: *Ephesians 1:9-11.*
replacement: *Ephesians 1:9–11.* “And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will.” The Greek of verse 9: *kata tēn eudokian autou hēn proetheto en autō*; of verse 11: *prooristhentes kata prothesin tou ta panta energountos kata tēn boulēn tou thelēmatos autou*.

contains: *The comprehensive sense — flourishing and welfare.*
replacement: *The comprehensive sense — flourishing and welfare.* Isaiah 26:3 — “You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You.” Isaiah 32:17 — “The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever.” Isaiah 53:5 — “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.” Jeremiah 29:11 records God's plans for His people: “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.” The comprehensive well-being belongs to God's people.

contains: *Zechariah 8:8* —
replacement: *Zechariah 8:8* — the post-exilic promise. “I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem, where they will be My people, and I will be their faithful and righteous God.”

*Matthew 23:13–15.* “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.” The Greek of verse 15: *poiēsai hena prosēlyton, kai hotan genētai, poieite auton huion geennēs diplotēron hymōn*.

contains: *The antinomian misreading.*
replacement: *The antinomian misreading.* Some Christian traditions, especially in popular evangelical Protestantism, have inferred from passages like Romans 6:14 (“you are not under law, but under grace”) that the law no longer has any claim on the believer’s conduct. They treat the Christian as free from the law in a way that means free from any obligation to its commands. The New Testament will not bear this. Christ redeems us *from* the law’s curse (Galatians 3:13) and *from* slavery to *anomia* (Titus 2:14), but not from the obligation to obedient love of God and neighbor. The Lutheran tradition has consistently resisted antinomianism — most famously in the antinomian controversies of the 1530s and 1540s, which produced the careful treatment of the law in the Formula of Concord.

contains: Throughout the New Testament, the same connection runs.
replacement: Throughout the New Testament, the same connection runs. The Romans letter, the densest theological exposition in the Pauline corpus, opens and closes with the same phrase: *hypakoē pisteōs* — “the obedience that comes from faith” (Romans 1:5; 16:26, BSB). The phrase bookends the whole letter. Paul's apostolic mission is *eis hypakoēn pisteōs* — for the obedience of faith among all the nations. The faith Paul proclaims is the faith that obeys; the obedience the gospel produces is the obedience that flows from faith. The two are not separable. The believer who has heard the gospel rightly is the believer who lives in obedience.

contains: The passage develops the believer's obedience as the inner reality
replacement: The passage develops the believer's obedience as the inner reality of Christian existence. The believer “wholeheartedly obeyed” (*ek kardias*) “the form of teaching” (*typon didachēs*) to which he was committed. The obedience is not externally imposed compliance but inner allegiance — the heart's submission to the gospel.

contains: *The fruit of evangelistic and pastoral labor.*
replacement: *The fruit of evangelistic and pastoral labor.* Romans 1:13 — Paul's desire for "some fruit" among the Romans. Philippians 1:22 — “fruitful labor for me.” Colossians 1:6 — the gospel "bearing fruit" in the world.

contains: Third, the believer's "Amen" through Christ.
replacement: Third, the believer's "Amen" through Christ. *Dio kai di' autou to amēn tō theō pros doxan di' hēmōn* — “through Him, our ‘Amen’ is spoken to the glory of God.” Because all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ, the believer responds with "Amen" — the affirmation of faith — through Christ, to the glory of God. The structure is beautiful: God says "Yes" to His promises in Christ; the believer says "Amen" to God's "Yes," through Christ, for God's glory. The divine "Yes" and the human "Amen" meet in Christ.

contains: Yet the New Testament uses *proselytos* only four times.
replacement: Yet the New Testament uses *proselytos* only four times. Once in the Gospels (Matthew 23:15 — Jesus's stinging rebuke of the Pharisees who “traverse land and sea to win a single convert”). Three times in Acts (2:11 — the proselytes at Pentecost; 6:5 — Nicolas of Antioch; 13:43 — the devout proselytes at Pisidian Antioch). And then the word essentially disappears from the New Testament's developed theological vocabulary. Paul, who wrote more about the Gentile inclusion than any other apostle, never uses *proselytos*. Peter, who wrote substantially about the church as the people of God, never uses *proselytos*. John, who developed the theology of the Word made flesh and the Spirit's work in believers, never uses *proselytos*.

contains: *2 Chronicles 8:14* —
replacement: *2 Chronicles 8:14* — Solomon's appointment of the priests' service: “In keeping with the ordinances of his father David, Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests over their service, and the Levites for their duties to offer praise and to minister before the priests according to the daily requirement.” The cultic *leitourgia* has a particular form established by authority and continued faithfully.

contains: *The relational sense — wholeness of relationships.*
replacement: *The relational sense — wholeness of relationships.* Genesis 26:29–31 — Isaac and Abimelech making peace through covenant. Second Samuel 17:3 — Ahithophel's counsel that “all the people will be at peace.” The harmony of human relationships.
